content: Campylobacter is a genus of Gram-negative, spiral-shaped, microaerophilic bacteria. These organisms are motile, possessing either single or bipolar flagella, which contribute to their characteristic curved, rod-like appearance. They are oxidase-positive. Among the species within this genus, Campylobacter jejuni is now recognized as one of the leading causes of bacterial foodborne illnesses in many developed nations. At least twelve species of Campylobacter have been implicated in human diseases, with C. jejuni and C. coli being the most prevalent. Additionally, C. fetus is known to cause spontaneous abortions in cattle and sheep and can act as an opportunistic pathogen in humans. The genomes of several Campylobacter species have been sequenced, offering valuable insights into their pathogenic mechanisms. These bacteria possess two flagellin genes, flaA and flaB, arranged in tandem, which are essential for motility. Intergenic recombination between these genes enhances their virulence. Notably, non-motile mutants of Campylobacter are unable to colonize their hosts, underscoring the importance of motility in their pathogenicity. Campylobacteriosis refers to an infection caused by Campylobacter species. The primary routes of transmission include the fecal-oral route, person-to-person sexual contact, and the ingestion of contaminated food or water. The infection typically manifests as an inflammatory diarrhea, which may be bloody, and is often accompanied by symptoms such as abdominal cramps, fever, and pain. In some cases, it may present as periodontitis or a dysentery-like syndrome. The disease is usually self-limiting, and symptomatic treatment involving fluid and electrolyte replacement is sufficient in most cases. The use of antibiotics remains a subject of debate. The most common causative agent of campylobacteriosis is C. jejuni, a spiral or comma-shaped bacterium that is non-pathogenic in its natural hosts, such as cattle, swine, and birds. Other species, including C. coli (also found in cattle, swine, and birds), C. upsaliensis (found in cats and dogs), and C. lari (commonly present in seabirds), can also cause the disease. The pathogenic effects of Campylobacter infections are primarily due to tissue injury in the gastrointestinal tract, particularly in the jejunum, ileum, and colon. C. jejuni achieves this by invading and destroying epithelial cells. Some strains of C. jejuni produce a cholera-like enterotoxin, which contributes to the watery diarrhea observed in infections. The organism also induces diffuse, bloody, edematous, and exudative enteritis. In rare cases, the infection may be associated with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) or thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) through mechanisms that are not yet fully understood. The differential diagnosis of Campylobacter infections involves distinguishing them from other causes of viral, bacterial, and parasitic gastroenteritis. Small bowel diarrhea caused by Campylobacter is typically watery and voluminous, with fewer than five white blood cells (WBCs) per high-power field on microscopy. In contrast, large bowel diarrhea is characterized by mucus and/or blood, lower stool volume, and more than ten WBCs per high-power field. In immunocompromised patients, the WBC count in stool samples can be significantly higher, sometimes reaching up to 1000 WBCs per high-power field. These findings help differentiate inflammatory causes of chronic diarrhea. A 3D computer-generated image of a cluster of drug-resistant Campylobacter bacteria is available in the Public Health Image Library (PHIL).
